title: Detailed-route congestion in SRAM channels fixed with channel-local routing blockages and incremental placement instead of floorplan rework
design_context: 28nm, 1.05M placeable instances, 78 SRAM hard macros, 5 clock domains, commercial synthesis + commercial P&R
prior_state: Post-CTS optimization clean: WNS -0.021 ns, TNS -1.2 ns, global-route overflow 0.3% (within tolerance), utilization 72%. First detailed-route attempt then failed: 3,900 DRC shorts, global-route overflow re-estimated at 3.1%, concentrated in the macro-to-macro channels (six channels held ~70% of the overflow), not uniformly distributed.
observation: First detailed-route run: 3,900 shorts plus antenna/markup errors clustered in six SRAM channels; overflow map showed local 10-15% hotspots in those channels against <0.5% elsewhere. severity: HIGH
hypothesis: Global route's coarse estimates hid that the channels had insufficient low-layer (M2-M4) track supply for the pin-side detour routing detailed route actually performs; placement had legally packed standard cells right up to the macro edges, consuming the channels' access tracks. Because the hotspots were channel-local rather than uniform, a global intervention (utilization, full re-place) would spend schedule without addressing the track-supply mismatch where it mattered.

candidates_considered.action: Shift two SRAM rows to widen the worst channels
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Macro positions were signed off against the top-level pin assignment and power grid; moving them reopens the top-level integration review and forces a full re-place/re-CTS — estimated 10-12 working days against a tape-in checkpoint in 4 weeks.

candidates_considered.action: Drop block utilization from 72% to ~62% and re-place everything
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Block boundary is frozen by the chip floorplan; lower utilization means a larger block area, which the top level cannot absorb, and a full re-place invalidates the clean post-CTS timing anyway.

candidates_considered.action: Turn up routing effort/layer-tapering globally and iterate detailed route
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Two overnight attempts already showed shorts moving around rather than clearing (3,900 → 3,100 → 3,350); pure effort escalation burns 2 days of machine time while the track-supply problem stays.

chosen_intervention: Kept the floorplan. (1) Added M2-M3 routing blockages inside the six worst channels to force the router to enter/exit macros on M4-M5 and to route channel-crossing nets on M5/M6. (2) Placed soft placement blockages (25% density cap) in a 3µm band around each macro edge so the next incremental placement pull-out cells congesting the channel mouths. (3) Ran one incremental congestion-driven placement pass with those constraints, then re-ran detailed route.
post_state: Overflow 3.1% → 0.5%, DRC 3,900 → 210 (metal shorts near pin access, closed by targeted ECOs within 2 days). Timing paid a small, expected cost: WNS -0.021 → -0.033 ns, TNS -1.2 → -3.9 ns from longer pin-side detours; accepted at signoff margins. Utilization effectively unchanged at 72.3% after the soft blockages. Total elapsed cost: 3 days, no floorplan or CTS redo.
expert_assessment: Right call: channel-concentrated overflow with a clean post-CTS map is the classic hidden-track-supply signature, and layer/blockage surgery inside the channels is cheap and reversible while macro moves are neither. The lesson is to check WHERE overflow sits before deciding between local and structural fixes. It would NOT transfer to a block with uniform overflow at high utilization — there the utilization/floorplan really is the problem and blockages just relocate the shortage.
weakest_point: The 3-day, one-pass incremental placement recovery is optimistic; real flows usually need two or three placement/route iterations before the shorts stop migrating.

title: 1,900 setup paths failing 150-250 ps from one launch bank read as a logic-depth problem — fixed by restructuring, not by pushing placement
design_context: 16nm, 2.1M placeable instances, 110 macros, 2 clock domains (960 MHz core, 400 MHz peripheral), commercial synthesis + commercial P&R
prior_state: Post-route setup: WNS -0.19 ns, TNS -310 ns, 1,870 failing endpoints all in the 960 MHz domain; utilization 68%; hold clean (+0.008 ns); DRC 60.
observation: The report shape: 1,870 paths failing by a tight 150-250 ns-ps band (150-250 ps), every path launched from one 300-bit register bank, all sharing the same deep datapath cone through a serial priority chain before diverging to scattered endpoints. Placement of the endpoints was not correlated with failure severity — near and far endpoints failed by the same amount. severity: CRITICAL
hypothesis: Uniform large-magnitude failure independent of endpoint placement location means the slack is consumed before placement matters: this is a logic-depth problem (the priority chain's depth exceeds the cycle budget), not a physical wire problem and not a constraint artifact — pushing the physical engine harder can buy tens of picoseconds at best against a ~200 ps structural deficit.

candidates_considered.action: More placement/timing optimization effort: bind the cone tighter, upscale gates, push the router
candidates_considered.rejected_because: On logic-limited paths the physical engine typically recovers 30-50 ps; the deficit is ~200 ps, so this burns 2-3 days of iterations and leaves the block fundamentally unclosable.

candidates_considered.action: Treat it as a constraint problem and relax the clock or claim the paths false
candidates_considered.rejected_because: The paths are real same-edge transfers on the operating frequency promised in the spec; relaxing SDC hides the deficit and moves the failure to silicon or to the SoC integration schedule.

candidates_considered.action: Pipeline the cone with a new register stage at the cone output
candidates_considered.rejected_because: A visible pipeline register changes the block's cycle-accurate interface contract (one-cycle latency on the bank's outputs), rippling into the block-level verification environment and the receiving block — a 4-6 week churn, too late for this revision.

chosen_intervention: Logic restructuring in synthesis, invisible at the block interface: replaced the serial priority chain with a parallel (one-hot select) structure and applied register retiming WITHIN the cone (balanced pipeline registers already existed mid-cone), letting synthesis move them forward. No port-level behavior change, so the verification environment and the neighbor contract were untouched. One synthesis loop plus incremental place-and-route.
post_state: WNS -0.19 → -0.038 ns, TNS -310 → -28 ns, failing endpoints 1,870 → 240 (the remainder are genuinely physical-limited paths near placement hotspots, closable by ordinary ECO). Hold re-checked after retiming: +0.008 → +0.002 ns, still met. Area +1.8% from the parallel structure; utilization 68% → 69.2%. Elapsed cost: 4 days.
expert_assessment: The shape-reading was the whole game: many paths, similar large magnitude, shared launch bank, no placement correlation — that signature points at logic depth, and only restructuring pays against it. The general lesson is to classify the failure (constraint vs. logic vs. physical) from the report before spending machine time. It would NOT transfer to the opposite shapes: few paths failing slightly points at physical/ECO, and violations that appear only under one analysis mode usually point at constraints.
weakest_point: Retiming recovering ~150 ps without changing the visible interface is the most optimistic link; most real cones give up less before setup/hold balance and gate-upsizing limits bite.

title: Slow config-register bus given an evidence-backed 2-cycle multicycle instead of a single-cycle budget that would have forced pipelining
design_context: 12nm, sub-block of 900k instances, 45 macros, 900 MHz core domain plus a 100 MHz configuration domain crossing into a neighbor block over a 512-bit register-style configuration bus, commercial STA + commercial synthesis
prior_state: Interface timing under the initial handoff SDC (single-cycle 900 MHz assumption on the config bus): WNS -0.24 ns at the boundary, TNS -96 ns across 512 endpoint bits; inner-block logic otherwise closing at +0.015 ns.
observation: All 512 boundary paths failed by 220-260 ps, but only on the config bus; every other cross-block path met. The bus had a documented strobe-based write protocol where data is captured only when a write-enable pulse is asserted, and the protocol guaranteed data stable for at least 8 cycles of the 900 MHz clock before any capture. severity: MODERATE
hypothesis: The violations were a constraint artifact: the single-cycle assumption asserted a same-edge transfer the hardware protocol never performs, so STA was checking a path that cannot be exercised. With a documented 2-cycle (minimum) data-stable window, the honest constraint is a 2-cycle setup multicycle with a matched hold exception — not a physical redesign.

candidates_considered.action: Keep single-cycle and pipeline the bus at the boundary to meet 900 MHz
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Two pipeline stages on a 512-bit bus cost real area (~6k cells), push the inner block over its power budget, and — decisive — change the write latency the configuration protocol documents, forcing re-verification of every register access sequence on both blocks (weeks of churn) to satisfy a constraint for a transfer that does not exist.

candidates_considered.action: Fix it physically: harder optimization, cell upsizing on the 512 paths
candidates_considered.rejected_because: A 240 ps deficit at the boundary is far beyond ECO-scale recovery (tens of ps); it would leave the interface red at signoff while consuming days of iterations.

candidates_considered.action: Waive the paths as false paths with no documentation
candidates_considered.rejected_because: An undocumented exception is indistinguishable from a mistake at the next re-derivation; the SDC loses provenance and the waiver silently breaks if the write protocol ever changes.

chosen_intervention: Derived the exception from the protocol, not from the timing number: got the bus owner's written confirmation of the strobe-based capture and the minimum stable window, added a formal check that write-enable cannot assert within one cycle of a data change, then wrote set_multicycle_path 2 -setup (with the matching hold multicycle) scoped exactly to the 512 config-bus paths, documenting owner, protocol reference, and date in an SDC comment block above the exception.
post_state: Interface WNS -0.24 → +0.31 ns, TNS -96 → 0 ns on those paths; every other path in the block unchanged (+0.015 ns). No area or power change. The exception survived two later SDC re-derivations by other engineers because its provenance block named the protocol owner.
expert_assessment: Right call: the number of failing bits matching the bus width exactly, with everything else green, is the constraint-artifact signature, and the fix belongs in the SDC with documented provenance rather than in silicon. The lesson: an exception is only as good as the evidence attached to it — the formal check is what made this an engineering decision instead of a fudge. It would NOT transfer to a bus without a strobe/guarantee mechanism: if capture really can happen any cycle, single-cycle analysis is correct and only pipelining is honest.
weakest_point: The formal 'write-enable cannot assert early' check is the fragile claim — most real config protocols rely on driver convention rather than a provable property, so the evidence step is where this story is most likely to fail review.
